_comment: Supplemental items, RN batch 04: Management of Care, Safety and Infection Control, and Psychosocial Integrity. Pilot status.

questions.stem: The nurse on an antepartum unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: New bright red bleeding in a client with placenta previa can quickly become a hemorrhage that threatens both the client and the fetus, so this client needs immediate assessment. A normal fasting glucose, tolerating breakfast with hyperemesis, and irregular Braxton Hicks contractions near term are stable findings.

options.text: A client at 33 weeks with placenta previa who reports a new gush of bright red, painless bleeding
A client at 28 weeks with gestational diabetes whose fasting glucose this morning was 92 mg/dL
A client at 30 weeks with hyperemesis who kept down crackers and juice at breakfast
A client at 36 weeks who reports Braxton Hicks contractions off and on today

questions.stem: The occupational health nurse at a manufacturing plant receives four requests at once. Which worker needs the nurse's response first?
questions.rationale: Alkaline chemicals penetrate eye tissue quickly and can cause permanent damage, so immediate, continuous irrigation is needed. Discussing screening results, a minor cut, and a vaccination are not urgent.

options.text: A worker who wants to discuss the results of a hearing screening done last month at the plant
A worker with a paper cut who is asking for a bandage
A worker who needs a flu shot
A worker who splashed an alkaline cleaning solution into one eye

questions.topic: Illegal substances in a client's belongings
questions.stem: While listing a newly admitted client's belongings, the nurse finds a bag of what appears to be illegal drugs. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Facilities have policies for suspected illegal substances, which usually call for securing the item, notifying security, and documenting objectively, without the nurse searching further or confronting the client. Returning the drugs creates a safety risk for the client and others, and destroying them is not the nurse's decision.

options.text: Return the bag to the client's belongings, since the client's property is private and protected by law
Follow facility policy, which usually involves notifying security and securing the bag
Flush the contents down the toilet right away so that no one else on the unit can use them
Let the client keep it

questions.topic: Law enforcement requests for blood samples
questions.stem: A police officer asks the nurse to draw a blood alcohol sample from a conscious, competent client involved in a car crash. The client refuses. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Drawing blood from a competent client who refuses, without a warrant, court order, or other legal authority, can be battery. The nurse follows facility policy, which usually involves the supervisor or risk management. A police request alone does not override the client's refusal, deceiving the client is unethical, and the officer cannot perform the procedure.

options.text: Draw the sample, since a police officer has the authority to request it from any client
Draw the sample while the client is distracted so that the client does not become upset
Not draw blood without consent, a warrant, or another legal basis per policy
Ask the officer to draw the sample personally, since nurses are not allowed to be involved

questions.topic: Assignments for a nurse in orientation
questions.stem: The charge nurse is choosing a client for a newly licensed nurse in the second week of orientation with a preceptor. Which client is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Early in orientation, a new nurse should care for stable clients with predictable needs while building skills with the preceptor. A client on a vasopressor after an ICU transfer, a client with a new tracheostomy who needs frequent suctioning, and a client with worsening alcohol withdrawal are unstable or high risk.

options.text: A client with sepsis on a vasopressor who arrived from the ICU an hour ago
A stable client 2 days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy who needs teaching
A client with a new tracheostomy who needs frequent suctioning
A client in alcohol withdrawal whose symptom score is rising

questions.stem: The nurse educator teaches staff to use a new IV infusion pump. Which method best evaluates whether staff can use the pump correctly?
questions.rationale: A psychomotor skill is best evaluated by observing the learner perform it, so a return demonstration shows whether each nurse can program the pump correctly. Attendance, knowledge of pump history, and self-reported confidence do not show competence.

options.text: Having each nurse sign an attendance sheet at the end of the education session on the pump
Giving a written test on pump history
Asking whether staff feel confident
Having each nurse program the pump during a return demonstration

questions.stem: A competent client recovering from a stroke wants to go home rather than to the skilled nursing facility the team recommends. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: A competent client has the right to make decisions that the team would not choose. The nurse supports the decision and helps plan the safest discharge, such as home health services, equipment, and family support. Misstating insurance rules, seeking a finding of incompetence because the team disagrees, and delaying discharge to pressure the client do not respect autonomy.

options.text: Tell the client that the team's recommendation must be followed for insurance to pay for care
Ask the provider to declare the client incompetent so the family can decide for them
Respect the choice and work with the team to plan the safest discharge home
Delay discharge until the client agrees

questions.stem: A client with a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order is scheduled for surgery to repair a hip fracture. Which action reflects current guidelines?
questions.rationale: Current guidelines call for required reconsideration: a DNR order is neither automatically suspended nor ignored during surgery. The surgeon and anesthesia team discuss with the client or surrogate which interventions are acceptable during the procedure, and the plan is documented. Clients with DNR orders can have surgery, and the anesthesia team must know the client's wishes.

options.text: Make sure the team discusses the DNR order with the client before surgery
Suspend the DNR order automatically for the entire perioperative period without a discussion
Cancel the surgery, since clients with DNR orders cannot undergo any procedures
Keep the DNR order in place without telling the anesthesia team anything about it

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes is overwhelmed by the information given in the hospital. Which referral will best support ongoing self-management?
questions.rationale: Diabetes self-management education and support programs teach skills over time, such as glucose monitoring, medication use, nutrition, and problem solving, which is more effective than teaching everything during a hospital stay. A home health aide cannot give medications, and physical therapy and hospice do not address the client's learning needs.

options.text: A home health aide to give all of the client's medications each day
A diabetes self-management education and support program after discharge
A physical therapist for a strengthening program at home
A hospice program for symptom management

questions.topic: Speaking up during a surgical time-out
questions.stem: During a time-out, the nurse notices that the surgical site marked on the client does not match the consent form. The surgeon says to proceed. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Under the Universal Protocol, any team member can stop a procedure when there is a safety concern. If a first concern is dismissed, the nurse states it again clearly (the two-challenge rule) and uses the chain of command if needed. Proceeding risks wrong-site surgery, documenting afterward does not prevent harm, and an anesthetized client cannot answer.

options.text: Restate the concern and stop the procedure until the discrepancy is resolved
Proceed as directed, since the surgeon is responsible for knowing the correct surgical site
Document the discrepancy after the case
Ask the anesthetized client

questions.stem: The nurse on a cardiac unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: A growing swelling at the femoral access site suggests a hematoma from bleeding, which needs immediate pressure, assessment of distal pulses and vital signs, and notification of the provider. A question about daily weights, a scheduled stress test, and a menu request can wait.

options.text: A client with heart failure who asks why a daily weight is needed every single morning before breakfast
A client with stable angina who is scheduled for an exercise stress test early tomorrow morning
A client with hypertension asking for a menu
A client 2 hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization with a growing groin swelling

questions.stem: A provider stops the nurse in the hallway and verbally prescribes a stool softener for a client. It is not an emergency, and the provider can use the electronic order system. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Verbal prescriptions increase the risk of errors, so policies limit them to emergencies or situations in which the provider cannot enter them. When the provider can use the electronic system, the nurse asks the provider to enter the prescription. Notes on scraps of paper, delayed signatures, and relying on another nurse's memory invite errors.

options.text: Write the prescription on a paper towel and enter it into the client's record later in the shift
Give the stool softener now and ask the provider to sign for it at the end of the week
Ask the provider to enter the prescription in the electronic record
Ask another nurse to remember the prescription and enter it into the record at a later time

questions.stem: The nurse on a bariatric surgery unit is caring for four clients on the first day after surgery. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.rationale: Persistent tachycardia, new left shoulder pain, and restlessness after bariatric surgery can be early signs of an anastomotic leak or pulmonary embolism, both of which need urgent evaluation. Mild pain, following the prescribed fluid schedule, and questions about the diet are expected.

options.text: A client who reports mild incisional pain and wants to know when walking is allowed
A client who is sipping 30 mL of water every 15 minutes as prescribed
A client with a heart rate of 124/min, new left shoulder pain, and increasing restlessness
A client who asks when pureed foods can be started after discharge

questions.stem: Which outcomes are considered nurse-sensitive quality indicators? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Nurse-sensitive indicators reflect the structure, process, and outcomes of nursing care, such as pressure injuries, falls with injury, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, and restraint use. Insurance status and the number of later office visits are not measures of nursing care quality.

options.text: Hospital-acquired pressure injuries
Falls with injury
Catheter-associated urinary tract infections
The client's insurance status
Physical restraint prevalence
The number of provider office visits after discharge

questions.topic: Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
questions.stem: A client with chest pain and no health insurance arrives at the emergency department. Which actions comply with the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA)? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: EMTALA requires hospitals with emergency departments to provide a medical screening examination and stabilizing treatment regardless of ability to pay, and to arrange appropriate transfer only when the hospital cannot provide the needed care. Delaying screening to ask about payment and transferring a client because of a lack of insurance violate the law.

options.text: Providing a medical screening examination
Stabilizing the client's emergency condition before any transfer
Arranging an appropriate transfer only if the hospital cannot provide needed care
Asking about payment before the screening examination
Sending the client to a public hospital because of a lack of insurance

questions.stem: Under HIPAA, which rights do clients have regarding their health information? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: HIPAA gives clients the right to access their records, request amendments, receive an accounting of certain disclosures, and request confidential communications. A request for amendment can be denied and does not delete the original entry, and clients cannot view another person's record without authorization.

options.text: Getting a copy of their medical record
Requesting corrections to information they believe is wrong
Receiving a list of certain disclosures of their information
Asking to be contacted at an alternative address or phone number
Having any entry they disagree with deleted from the record
Viewing a family member's record without permission

questions.stem: For each response to a conflict between two nurses about holiday scheduling, indicate the conflict management strategy it reflects.
questions.rationale: Avoiding sidesteps the conflict. Accommodating sets aside one's own needs for the other person's. Compromising means each side gives up something to reach an acceptable middle ground. Collaborating means working together toward a solution that satisfies both parties and is usually the most effective long-term approach.

rows.text: One nurse says nothing and hopes the issue goes away
One nurse gives up the request so the other can have the holiday off
Each nurse works half of the holiday
The nurses work together to find a solution that fully meets both of their needs
The nurses agree that each will give up one preferred day

questions.answer_summary: One nurse says nothing and hopes the issue goes away: Avoiding; One nurse gives up the request so the other can have the holiday off: Accommodating; Each nurse works half of the holiday: Compromising; The nurses work together to find a solution that fully meets both of their needs: Collaborating; The nurses agree that each will give up one preferred day: Compromising

questions.stem: For each quality improvement purpose, indicate the most appropriate tool.
questions.rationale: A root cause analysis looks back at an event to find system causes. A failure mode and effects analysis looks ahead at a new process to find where it could fail. A run chart shows data over time to reveal trends. A fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram organizes possible causes of a problem into categories.

rows.text: Analyze why a sentinel event occurred after it happened
Predict how a new medication process could fail before it is put in place
Track the unit's monthly fall rate over a year
Sort possible causes of medication delays into categories such as people, equipment, and methods
Display weekly hand hygiene compliance over time

questions.answer_summary: Analyze why a sentinel event occurred after it happened: Root cause analysis; Predict how a new medication process could fail before it is put in place: Failure mode and effects analysis; Track the unit's monthly fall rate over a year: Run chart; Sort possible causes of medication delays into categories such as people, equipment, and methods: Fishbone diagram; Display weekly hand hygiene compliance over time: Run chart

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Lewin's model has three stages. Unfreezing creates readiness by showing why the current approach needs to change, moving puts the change into practice, and refreezing builds the change into routines and policies so that it lasts.
questions.template: According to Lewin's change theory, the nurse manager first ___1___ by helping staff see why a change is needed, and the change becomes lasting during the ___2___ stage.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: An institutional review board reviews research involving human participants to protect their rights and safety. Participation is voluntary, so participants may withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of the care they would otherwise receive.
questions.template: Before a study involving human participants begins, it must be approved by ___1___, and a participant who has given consent ___2___.

options: may withdraw at any time without losing access to usual care
must stay in the study until it ends
may withdraw only with the researcher's permission
blanks.correct: may withdraw at any time without losing access to usual care

questions.answer_summary: 1: an institutional review board; 2: may withdraw at any time without losing access to usual care

questions.stem: The charge nurse is reviewing a client's data before assigning the client to an LPN/VN. Highlight the findings that indicate the client should instead be assigned to an RN.
questions.rationale: A recent ICU transfer and falling oxygen saturation make the client's condition unstable and unpredictable, and initial teaching is an RN responsibility, so the client should be assigned to an RN. Scheduled oral medications, a simple dressing change, and walking with standby assistance are within the LPN/VN's scope.

passage_segments.text: Transferred from the ICU 1 hour ago.
SpO2 dropped from 96% to 89% in the last hour.
Needs initial teaching for a new insulin regimen.
Has a clean, dry incision that needs a daily dressing change.
Walks to the bathroom with standby assistance.

questions.correct_text: Transferred from the ICU 1 hour ago; SpO2 dropped from 96% to 89% in the last hour; Needs initial teaching for a new insulin regimen
questions.answer_summary: Transferred from the ICU 1 hour ago; SpO2 dropped from 96% to 89% in the last hour; Needs initial teaching for a new insulin regimen

questions.stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions while wearing gloves, a gown, a surgical mask, and goggles. Which item should the nurse remove first?
questions.rationale: Gloves are the most contaminated item, so they are removed first (or together with the gown), followed by the goggles, gown, and then the mask, which is removed last by the ties or ear loops. Hand hygiene is performed immediately after removing all PPE and whenever the hands become contaminated.

options.text: The gloves
The goggles
The gown
The mask

questions.stem: Before entering the room of a client with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, the nurse puts on a fit-tested N95 respirator. What should the nurse do next?
questions.rationale: A user seal check is done every time an N95 respirator is put on to make sure air is not leaking around the edges. The nosepiece is molded firmly to the nose, the top strap goes over the crown of the head and the bottom strap at the back of the neck, and annual fit testing does not replace the seal check.

options.text: Pinch the nosepiece loosely so the respirator is comfortable to wear during the visit
Pull the bottom strap over the top of the head and the top strap under the ears
Skip the seal check, since the respirator was fit-tested
Perform a user seal check by exhaling and inhaling to detect leaks

questions.stem: The home health nurse is visiting an 80-year-old client who lives alone. Which recommendation best reduces the client's risk of falling at home?
questions.rationale: Throw rugs are a common tripping hazard, and night-lights improve visibility during nighttime trips to the bathroom. Items on high shelves lead to climbing and reaching, backless slippers can slide off, and anything stored on stairs is a tripping hazard.

options.text: Keep frequently used items on high shelves to save floor space
Remove throw rugs and add night-lights
Wear soft slippers without backs for comfort around the house
Store a few pairs of shoes on the stairs so they are easy to reach

questions.stem: Parents of a 14-month-old ask when their child can ride in a forward-facing car seat. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Current recommendations are to keep children rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the highest height or weight allowed by the car seat, which for most children is well past age 2. Legs touching the vehicle seat are not a safety concern. Sitting unsupported and walking are not criteria for turning the seat, and booster seats are for much older children.

options.text: Turn the seat to face forward on the child's first birthday, since the legs are now too long
Keep the child rear-facing as long as possible, until the seat's height or weight limit is reached
Turn the seat forward once the child can sit up without support and hold up the head
Use a booster seat with the vehicle's lap and shoulder belt once the child walks

questions.stem: A confused older client keeps trying to climb out of bed. Which action by the nurse is safest?
questions.rationale: A low bed, a bed alarm, frequent checks, and meeting needs such as toileting are the least restrictive ways to prevent falls. Four raised side rails act as a restraint, and a confused client may climb over them and fall from a greater height or become trapped. Tight sheets restrict movement, and a dark room increases confusion and fall risk.

options.text: Raise all four side rails so the client cannot get out of bed without help from staff
Tuck the sheets tightly
Keep the room dark
Lower the bed, use a bed alarm, and check on the client frequently

questions.stem: A single-dose vial still contains some medication after the nurse draws up the prescribed dose for a client. What should the nurse do with the vial?
questions.rationale: Single-dose vials do not contain preservatives and are meant for one client and one procedure. Saving or reusing the leftover medication has caused outbreaks of bloodstream infections and hepatitis, so the vial is discarded after one use.

options.text: Label it with the date and time and save it for the next client who needs the same drug
Store it in the refrigerator for use with this same client later in the week
Discard it, even though medication is left in the vial
Use it for the next client

questions.stem: When the nurse programs a heparin infusion, the smart pump alerts that the dose exceeds the hard limit in the drug library. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: A hard limit means the programmed dose is outside the safe range set for that drug and cannot be overridden. It usually signals a programming error, such as confusing units per hour with milliliters per hour, or a prescription error, so the nurse stops and verifies with the prescription, pharmacist, or provider. Bypassing the drug library removes the safety check.

options.text: Stop and recheck the prescription and programming
Override the alert, since smart pump limits are only suggestions that can be bypassed
Program the pump without the drug library so the alert does not appear again
Ask another nurse to override the alert using that nurse's own pump access code

questions.stem: Which measures support respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette in a clinic waiting room? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Signs, masks, tissues with no-touch disposal, and spatial separation reduce the spread of respiratory infections. Clients are taught to cough into a tissue or their elbow rather than their hands, and coughing clients are kept away from busy areas such as the reception desk.

options.text: Posting signs that ask clients with respiratory symptoms to tell staff
Offering masks to clients who are coughing
Providing tissues and no-touch waste containers
Seating coughing clients apart from others when possible
Asking coughing clients to cover their mouths with their hands
Seating coughing clients next to the reception desk

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching parents about firearm safety in a home with children. Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Storing firearms unloaded and locked, with ammunition locked separately, and asking about firearms in other homes reduce the risk of unintentional shootings and suicide. Children can find hidden firearms, and teaching young children about guns does not reliably prevent them from handling a gun they find.

options.text: Store firearms unloaded and locked
Store ammunition locked and separate from firearms
Ask about unsecured firearms in homes the child visits
Hide a loaded firearm on a high closet shelf
Teach young children to handle guns safely so locked storage is not needed

questions.stem: For each item, indicate the minimum level of reprocessing required before it is used for another client.
questions.rationale: Critical items that enter sterile tissue or the bloodstream, such as surgical instruments and biopsy forceps, must be sterilized. Semicritical items that contact mucous membranes, such as endoscopes and vaginal probes, need at least high-level disinfection. Noncritical items that touch only intact skin, such as blood pressure cuffs and stethoscopes, need low-level disinfection.

rows.text: Surgical instruments
A flexible endoscope
A blood pressure cuff
A stethoscope
Biopsy forceps that enter sterile tissue
A vaginal ultrasound probe

questions.answer_summary: Surgical instruments: Sterilization; A flexible endoscope: High-level disinfection; A blood pressure cuff: Low-level disinfection; A stethoscope: Low-level disinfection; Biopsy forceps that enter sterile tissue: Sterilization; A vaginal ultrasound probe: High-level disinfection

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.rationale: Breast milk is thawed in the refrigerator overnight or by placing the container in warm water. Thawing at room temperature allows bacteria to grow, and boiling water can damage the milk. Microwaving heats unevenly, creating hot spots that can burn the infant's mouth.
questions.template: Frozen breast milk should be thawed ___1___, and it should never be ___2___.

options: in the refrigerator or in a bowl of warm water
in a pot of boiling water
blanks.correct: in the refrigerator or in a bowl of warm water

options: swirled gently to mix the fat
fed to the infant after thawing

questions.answer_summary: 1: in the refrigerator or in a bowl of warm water; 2: heated in a microwave oven

questions.stem: During an electronic system downtime, the nurse reviews new handwritten prescriptions. Highlight the prescriptions that must be clarified with the provider before they are carried out.
questions.rationale: "U" is on the do-not-use list because it can be misread as 0 or 4, so the prescription must say "units." The furosemide prescription has no dose, and an as-needed morphine prescription must state the indication. The metoprolol, acetaminophen, and heparin prescriptions are complete.

passage_segments.text: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg by mouth twice daily.
Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for temperature above 101°F (38.3°C).
Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed.

questions.correct_text: Insulin regular 10 U subcutaneously now; Furosemide IV now; Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed
questions.answer_summary: Insulin regular 10 U subcutaneously now; Furosemide IV now; Morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed

questions.stem: A client with antisocial personality disorder compliments the nurse and asks for an exception to the unit's phone-use rules. What is the nurse's best response?
questions.rationale: Clients with antisocial personality disorder may use flattery to gain special treatment. Clear, consistent limits applied by all staff reduce manipulation. Granting exceptions reinforces the behavior, inviting the client to argue that the rules do not apply opens negotiation, and postponing the answer suggests the rule may change.

options.text: Restate the unit's phone rules calmly and apply them the same way as for other clients
Grant the exception, since the client has been cooperative and polite with staff
Ask the client to explain why they feel the rules do not apply
Tell the client the request will be discussed at the next meeting

questions.topic: Relapse prevention in substance use disorder
questions.stem: A client in early recovery from opioid use disorder asks the nurse how to avoid relapsing. Which response by the nurse is most helpful?
questions.rationale: Relapse prevention focuses on recognizing personal triggers, such as certain people, places, and emotions, and planning coping strategies and support, such as a sponsor, peer group, or counselor, along with continuing medication for opioid use disorder if prescribed. Trying not to think about using does not stop cravings, relapse is a common part of recovery from a chronic illness rather than proof that treatment failed, and isolation increases the risk of relapse.

options.text: "Just avoid thinking about using, and the cravings will stop on their own soon enough."
"A relapse would mean treatment has failed."
"Let's identify your triggers and plan who you can call when cravings start."
"Stay home alone for now."

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching progressive muscle relaxation to a client with generalized anxiety disorder. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Progressive muscle relaxation involves tensing one muscle group at a time for a few seconds and then releasing it, helping the client recognize and reduce tension. It works best when practiced regularly, not only during a crisis. Tensing everything at once and holding the breath work against relaxation.

options.text: Tense all of the muscles in the body at once and hold the tension for as long as possible
Practice only during a panic attack, since the technique will not help at other times
Hold the breath while tensing
Tense each muscle group for a few seconds, then relax it and notice the difference

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia has a flat affect, says very little, and stays in bed most of the day. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Negative symptoms such as flat affect, alogia, and avolition respond best to structure and small, achievable goals that build success. Leaving the client in bed reinforces withdrawal, leading a large meeting is too demanding at first, and calling the client lazy is judgmental and ignores that these are symptoms of the illness.

options.text: Let the client stay in bed, since the negative symptoms will resolve without intervention
Set small, achievable daily goals for self-care
Encourage the client to lead the evening community meeting for the whole unit
Confront the client about laziness so that they will feel motivated to get up

questions.topic: Signs of elder abuse or neglect
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult brought in by a family caregiver. Which findings may indicate abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Bruises in various stages of healing, especially on the upper arms where someone might grab, poor hygiene, a caregiver who will not let the client speak, and delays in seeking care are warning signs that need further assessment and reporting. Thin skin from aging and weight loss explained by a known illness with appropriate care are not, by themselves, signs of abuse.

options.text: Bruises in different stages of healing on the upper arms
Poor hygiene and soiled clothing
The caregiver insists on answering every question for the client
Unexplained delays in seeking care for an injury
Thin, fragile skin consistent with aging
Gradual weight loss with a documented cancer diagnosis and an appropriate care plan

questions.stem: A client with Alzheimer's disease becomes agitated and confused every evening. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: A predictable routine, brighter light in the late afternoon, a calm evening environment, and daytime activity reduce sundowning. Restraints increase agitation and injury, and repeatedly correcting a confused client can increase distress; calm redirection works better.

options.text: Keep a consistent daily routine
Increase lighting in the late afternoon
Reduce noise and activity in the evening
Encourage physical activity earlier in the day
Apply restraints during the evening hours
Correct the client firmly each time they are confused

questions.stem: For each way a client describes coping with stress, indicate whether it is adaptive or maladaptive.
questions.rationale: Adaptive coping, such as exercise, talking with supportive people, and journaling, reduces stress without causing new problems. Maladaptive coping, such as using alcohol to sleep, withdrawing from everyone, and emotional overeating, may bring short-term relief but creates new health and social problems.

rows.text: Going for a walk after a stressful day
Drinking alcohol every night to fall asleep
Talking with a friend about worries
Avoiding all social contact
Writing in a journal
Eating large amounts of food when upset

questions.answer_summary: Going for a walk after a stressful day: Adaptive; Drinking alcohol every night to fall asleep: Maladaptive; Talking with a friend about worries: Adaptive; Avoiding all social contact: Maladaptive; Writing in a journal: Adaptive; Eating large amounts of food when upset: Maladaptive
